title: Amos 8:1–14
context: A fourth vision shows a basket of summer fruit, and the LORD declares that the end has come on his people Israel and that he will not again pass by them. The LORD then exposes merchants who long for the new moon and Sabbath to be over so they can cheat with false measures and buy the poor for silver. He swears by the pride of Jacob never to forget their works and announces mourning, darkness at noon, and a famine of hearing the LORD’s words. Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as judgment on injustice joined to empty religion, and both read the famine of the word as a grave judgment, though they may differ in emphasis on why the word is withheld.

verses.text: Thus the Lord GOD showed me: behold, a basket of summer fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: Thus the Lord GOD showed me: behold, a basket of summer fruit. Arminian readers see a fourth vision that begins with an ordinary sight, much as the earlier visions did.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that summer fruit marks the end of the harvest season. The image of ripe fruit at season’s end prepares for the LORD’s explanation in the next verse.

verses.text: He said, “Amos, what do you see?” I said, “A basket of summer fruit.” Then the LORD said to me, “The end has come on my people Israel. I will not again pass by them any more.
verses.arminianNotes: The end has come on my people Israel. Arminian readers see the LORD explaining the vision to Amos, and once again declaring that he will not pass by them any more.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many readers find a wordplay in Hebrew between summer fruit and end, much as Jeremiah 1:11-12 joins an almond branch to the LORD’s watching over his word.

verses.text: The songs of the temple will be wailing in that day,” says the Lord GOD. “The dead bodies will be many. In every place they will throw them out with silence.
verses.arminianNotes: The songs of the temple will be wailing in that day, Arminian readers see joyful worship turned into lament as judgment falls, described without graphic detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the dead are many and are cast out in silence. The verse pictures a sorrow too deep for words in the day of judgment.

verses.text: Hear this, you who desire to swallow up the needy, and cause the poor of the land to fail,
verses.arminianNotes: Hear this, you who desire to swallow up the needy, Arminian readers see the LORD confronting those who exploit the poor of the land and cause them to fail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the charge echoes Amos’s earlier concern for justice (5:24). The LORD hears and takes up the cause of the needy against the powerful who oppress them.

verses.text: saying, ‘When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may market wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel large, and dealing falsely with balances of deceit;
verses.arminianNotes: saying, ‘When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell grain? Arminian readers see religious observance treated as an obstacle to profit, with merchants impatient for holy days to end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the false measures: making the ephah small and the shekel large. Dishonest trade and outward religious observance stand side by side in the same people.

verses.text: that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals, and sell the sweepings with the wheat?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals, Arminian readers see people reduced to commodities, a charge that echoes 2:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the selling of the sweepings with the wheat, cheating even in the grain itself. The verse shows how greed corrupts every part of trade.

verses.text: The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob, “Surely I will never forget any of their works.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob, Arminian readers see the LORD’s oath that he will never forget any of their works, a sober assurance that injustice will be judged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the pride of Jacob may refer to the LORD himself or, ironically, to Israel’s arrogance; readers differ. Either way the oath stresses certainty.

verses.text: Won’t the land tremble for this, and everyone mourn who dwells in it? Yes, it will rise up wholly like the River; and it will be stirred up and sink again, like the River of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Won’t the land tremble for this, Arminian readers see creation itself responding to injustice, the land heaving and sinking like the River of Egypt in its yearly flood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same image appears in 9:5. The rising and sinking of the River of Egypt pictures a land shaken to its foundations by the LORD’s judgment.

verses.text: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord GOD, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.
verses.arminianNotes: that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, Arminian readers see darkness in the clear day as a sign of judgment, recalling the day of the LORD as darkness (5:18, 20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some connect the verse with an eclipse in Amos’s time, while others read it as poetic imagery; the text does not settle the matter. The Judges 9:23 box treats the LORD bringing such disaster.

verses.text: I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will make you wear sackcloth on all your bodies, and baldness on every head. I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its end like a bitter day.
verses.arminianNotes: I will turn your feasts into mourning, Arminian readers see the feasts turned to lament and songs to wailing, a reversal of empty celebration, described without excess.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the comparison to the mourning for an only son, the deepest grief known in Israel. Sackcloth and baldness are signs of mourning, and the end is a bitter day.

verses.text: Behold, the days come,” says the Lord GOD, “that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the LORD’s words.
verses.arminianNotes: that I will send a famine in the land, Arminian readers see a famine not of bread but of hearing the LORD’s words, a judgment on a people who refused the word while it was offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Deuteronomy 8:3, man lives by every word that proceeds out of the LORD’s mouth. Shared ground: both read the loss of the word as a grave judgment, differing chiefly in emphasis.

verses.text: They will wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east; they will run back and forth to seek the LORD’s word, and will not find it.
verses.arminianNotes: They will wander from sea to sea, Arminian readers see the people searching too late, running back and forth to seek the LORD’s word and not finding it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that hearing the word is a gift God may withdraw in judgment. Both traditions read the verse as a warning to value the word while it is near.

verses.text: In that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will faint for thirst.
verses.arminianNotes: In that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will faint for thirst. Arminian readers see even the strongest and most promising of the people overcome in that day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the thirst may be literal, spiritual, or both, continuing the famine image of 8:11. The verse pictures the young and vigorous fainting.

verses.text: Those who swear by the sin of Samaria, and say, ‘As your god, Dan, lives,’ and, ‘As the way of Beersheba lives,’ they will fall, and never rise up again.”
verses.arminianNotes: Those who swear by the sin of Samaria, Arminian readers see judgment on those who swear by false gods at Dan and Beersheba, places associated with worship outside the LORD’s way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some hear in the sin of Samaria a reference to a deity, and 2 Kings 17:30 names Ashima among later gods there, though the link is uncertain. Dan had a golden calf (1 Kings 12:29).
